catalog_quote: I.2.3.1.1.3. Le système tonal Selon S. Mokrani (2016. 570), l’inventaire des réalisations tonales laissent entrevoir un système simple composé de deux tons simples et de deux tons modulés. - un registre haut, noté [ ́] - un registre bas, noté [ `] Les réalisations sur ces registres sont: - Haut abaissé, noté ↓H - Montant, noté [ ˇ] - Bas ponctuel, noté [ ^] ... I.2.3.1.2.3. Organisation des tonèmes Sur le plan tonal, le parler kele atteste deux registres tonals fondamentaux: - Un registre haut, noté H / ́/ - Un registre bas, noté B / ̀/ L’auteur relève une règle dîte de « polarité tonale ». Cette règle repose sur le fait qu’en T1, la tonalité n’est pas régulière. Les tonèmes alternent dans cette position en ce qu’en V1 le ton peut être soit haut, soit bas, toute chose qui n’est pas commune à d’autres langues bantu. Les exemples / ákyìŋ/ « cadavre » et /làkákè/ « bâton » illustrent cet état de faits où l’on note que la voyelle en V1 peut porter soit un ton haut, soit un ton bas sans aucun conditionnement relatif.

new_statements.translation: Organisation of tonemes. Tonally, Kele has two basic tone registers: a High register (H) and a Low register (L). The author [Mokrani] notes a rule called 'tonal polarity': in T1 [first stem position] tone is not regular; tonemes alternate in this position in that in V1 the tone may be either high or low, which is not common in other Bantu languages. The examples /ákyìŋ/ 'corpse' and /làkákè/ 'stick' illustrate this: the V1 vowel may bear either a high or a low tone without any conditioning.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kele is described as a two-tone (H/L) language with lexical tone on stem vowels; no word stress or accent position is stated. The only prosodic generalization beyond tone is group-level (B20): stem-final syllables are regularly Low-toned, which the author reads as a possible incipient shift toward an accentual system.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. (Preston & Best 1854: 21 mention a 'strong accent' carried by the perfect-tense form in -me, a morphological remark only.)
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern lexical tone on noun/verb stems in citation forms from wordlists; the 'processus accentuel' remark (p. 238) is a diachronic interpretation for the whole B20 group, not a synchronic stress rule for Kele.
new_statements.identity_note: Koumbi Mabiti's 'Kele (B22a)' data (via Mokrani 2016) are from Akele of the Moyen-Ogooué lakes region (Lambaréné/Belle-Vue area); he notes speakers report the Ngounié variety differs (metombolo). Preston & Best 1854 describe 'Bakele/Dikele' of the Gaboon (Como) estuary, the same language (kele1257, ISO keb) in a now-displaced 19th-c. location. Closely related Ungom/Ngom (B22b, ngom1270?) is treated separately in the thesis and by some authors as the same language.

sources.note: Sec. I.2.3.1 'Kele (B22a)', pp. 96-102, phonology explicitly taken from Mokrani 2016: 7 vowels, 19 consonants, CV syllable, all final vowels realized [ə]; tonal system = two registers H and L (realizations: downstepped H, rising, 'bas ponctuel'), plus a 'polarité tonale' remark that V1 tone is unpredictable. No statement on word stress/accent for Kele. Group-level diachronic remark p. 238: stem-final syllable is regularly Low across B20 and the facts 'pourraient conforter.. une évolution vers un processus accentuel' (citing Rekanga 2007, Dodo-Bounguendza 2010).

sources.note: Orthography section (pp. 5-6, paras 1-8) treats vowels, nasal vowels, consonants and clusters only; no paragraph on accent, stress or tone. Sole mention is incidental, p. 21 (potential mood, perfect in -me): 'But if the final letter of the present be ă or ĕ, it is changed into a, because it is difficult to give the strong accent of this tense on ă and ĕ.' No word-stress rule.
